## Sandbox

See [Sandbox](sandbox.md) for detailed behavior and security notes.

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| `sandbox.enabled` | `true` | Enable sandboxed execution. When enabled and the msb CLI or host virtualization is unavailable, sandbox startup fails rather than falling back to the host; set `false` to run worktree-only. |
| `sandbox.mode` | `"msb"` | Sandbox mode. `msb` is currently the only supported mode. A stale `"mode": "sbx"` from an older install is reported as a migration warning in the log and, when running in the TUI, as a toast. |
| `sandbox.image` | `"oc-forge-sandbox:latest"` | msb image reference used for sandboxed execution. |
| `sandbox.resources.memory` | `"8g"` | Memory the sandbox gets (`msb create -m`). There is no autoscaling, so size it for the heaviest command it will run or that command is OOM-killed. The `Host sandbox` menu can change it on a running host sandbox, which restarts it. |
| `sandbox.resources.cpus` | `"4"` | CPU count the sandbox gets (`msb create -c`; integer-only). The `Host sandbox` menu can change it on a running host sandbox, which restarts it. |
| `sandbox.resources.dockerDisk` | `"16g"` | Size of the dedicated block device backing the sandbox's in-VM Docker Engine data dir (`/var/lib/docker`, `--mount-named ...:kind=disk,size=<size>`). The disk is sparse, so the generous default costs no real disk up front. |
| `sandbox.resources.cacheDisk` | `"16g"` | Size of the dedicated block device backing the sandbox's tool/package cache directory (`/opt/forge/cache` — the pnpm store, npm, uv, pip, uv-managed Pythons, cargo registry/git, go modules; `--mount-named ...:kind=disk,size=<size>`). Sparse like `dockerDisk`, and it keeps unbounded caches off the small root filesystem. Reclaim it with `forge-cache-prune` inside the sandbox, which clears caches while preserving installed toolchains. |
| `sandbox.mountProjectReadonly` | `true` | Mount the source project read-only at its identical host path. |
| `sandbox.mounts` | `[]` | Additional host directories to mount at their identical host path. |
| `sandbox.autoApprovePermissions` | `true` | Resolve permission prompts to allow or deny in sessions whose shell runs in a sandbox, including a session sandboxed from the `Host sandbox` menu, using the same policy as per-session auto-approve (`autoApprove.deny` matches and OpenCode `deny` rules are denied; everything else, including explicit `ask` rules, is allowed). Set `false` to keep prompting in sandboxed sessions; a per-session `Toggle auto-approve` still applies. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md#permission-auto-approval). |
| `sandbox.network.allow` | `[]` | Egress allow-list applied at create time. An empty list or `*`/`**` wildcard allows public egress; concrete hosts enable deny-by-default with an allow rule per validated host. Secret destinations also contribute allowed hosts. `allowLan: true` additionally allows msb's private-address group, regardless of the host list. |
| `sandbox.network.env` | `[]` | Host environment variables to inject into the sandbox at create time as bare names (values never appear on forge's command line). |
| `sandbox.network.secrets` | `[]` | Host-held credentials bound at create time. Each entry names a host env var and the hosts allowed to receive its real value; the value never enters the guest. The named variable must be exported in the environment that launches opencode — a bound secret with a missing variable breaks every sandboxed shell command. |
| `sandbox.network.allowLan` | `false` | Allow the sandbox to reach private (LAN) address ranges, which msb blocks by default even when public egress is open. This exposes every service on your LAN to commands the agent runs. Applied at create time. |

The TUI execution dialog can override `sandbox.resources.*` and `sandbox.network.allowLan` per loop when launching in Loop mode; the overrides are persisted on the loop row and applied when its sandbox is created. See [TUI → Loop Settings](tui.md#loop-settings). The `Host sandbox` menu overrides CPUs, memory, and LAN access for the project's host sandbox; see [TUI → Host Sandbox Menu](tui.md#host-sandbox-menu).

### Sandbox network egress

`sandbox.network.allow`, plus the destination hosts of any configured secrets, controls the sandbox's outbound access. Restriction is opt-in: when nothing is configured — or the allow list contains `*`/`**` — and `allowLan` is false, Forge passes no network flags and msb's default allows public egress while blocking private ranges. With `allowLan: true`, Forge instead passes `--net public,private`. A wildcard entry overrides narrower entries in the same list. When at least one concrete host or secret destination is configured and no allow-all wildcard is present, Forge passes `--net-default deny` plus one `--net-rule allow@<host>` per validated host; `allowLan: true` additionally permits the entire private-address group.

- Invalid host entries are skipped and logged rather than failing the loop launch. Verified rejections include commas (a comma separates whole rule tokens, not hosts), port-qualified hosts (colon), `@`, a suffix with fewer than two labels (`*.example.com` is valid, `*.com` is rejected), and a bare single-label hostname (use `domain=myhost`). `domain=` and `suffix=` forms pass through. A wildcard in a secret's destination hosts stays invalid — those hosts declare where that secret may be sent, not global egress policy.
- If every configured host is invalid, Forge emits `--net-default deny` with no host allow rules rather than falling back to allow-all. With `allowLan: true`, the private-address group remains allowed.
- DNS is gateway-mediated and needs no rule; the old `--net-rule allow@dns` form was rejected by msb 0.6.8, and its presence made every sandbox creation fail.
- With the default `allowLan: false`, the host's loopback interface remains unreachable from inside the sandbox: `host.microsandbox.internal` and the gateway IP are both blocked, because the private range is not part of msb's `public` egress group. `allowLan: true` adds msb's `private` group (`--net public,private`, or `--net-rule allow@private` when an allow-list is active); see [Sandbox → LAN Access](sandbox.md#lan-access).
- Egress rules cannot be changed on a live sandbox (`msb modify` has no `--net-rule`), so a newly configured host requires recreating the sandbox.

### Sandbox secrets

Credentials that should never be readable inside the guest belong in `sandbox.network.secrets`, not `env`. msb keeps a host-side source reference, exposes a `$MSB_<ENV>` placeholder inside the sandbox, and substitutes the real value only for the listed hosts at the network boundary:

```jsonc
{
  "sandbox": {
    "network": {
      "secrets": [
        { "env": "GITHUB_TOKEN", "hosts": ["api.github.com"] }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Each named variable must be exported in the environment that **launches opencode**. Once a secret is bound, every `msb exec` fails with `invalid config: secret <name>: host environment variable <name> is not set` if the variable is absent from the invoking process's environment; because the shell shim inherits opencode's environment, a missing variable breaks every sandboxed shell command. Forge logs an explicit warning naming the variable.

Adopting an existing sandbox (for example after a plugin restart) converges the bound secrets with `msb modify` exactly once per adoption per plugin instance: `--secret <env>@<hosts>` refreshes the current value of every configured entry, and `--secret-rm <env>` drops entries that are no longer configured. A refresh failure blocks adoption without marking the sandbox converged, so a later startup can retry. The previous per-sandbox plaintext env file under `<dataDir>/sandbox-env/` is gone.

## Auto-Approve

`autoApprove` configures the deny list applied while per-session auto-approve is on (`Toggle auto-approve` in the TUI, see [TUI → Sidebar](tui.md#sidebar)).

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| `autoApprove.deny` | `[]` | Extra rules denied while auto-approving, using OpenCode permission `action`/`resource` wildcard syntax. A request matching any entry is denied. Explicit OpenCode `ask` rules are allowed; OpenCode `deny` rules still apply. Entries without a non-empty string `action` and `resource` (or a non-array value) are ignored with a startup warning. |

```jsonc
{
  "autoApprove": {
    "deny": [
      { "action": "shell", "resource": "rm -rf *" }
    ]
  }
}
```

> **Upgrade note.** Auto-approve now allows `ask` rules, including in already-enabled sessions. To preserve blocking, use explicit `deny` rules or `autoApprove.deny`.

## Bundled Assets & Installer

Forge ships editable assets that are installed into your config dir:

| Asset | Installed to | Manifest |
|---|---|---|
| Agent & command prompts | `~/.config/opencode/forge/prompts/` | `~/.config/opencode/forge/manifests/prompts.json` |
| Skills | `~/.config/opencode/skills/` | `~/.config/opencode/forge/manifests/skills.json` |
| Config | `~/.config/opencode/forge-config.jsonc` | — |

### Automatic startup sync

On every plugin load, Forge silently syncs bundled prompts and skills. The sync is non-destructive and tracks provenance by content hash in the manifests:

- **New file** → installed.
- **Unedited file, bundle changed** → refreshed to the new bundled version.
- **File you edited** → preserved; never overwritten.
- Files are **never deleted** by the startup sync.

Because edits are detected by comparing the file hash against the recorded manifest hash, you should never hand-edit a manifest. Setting a manifest hash to match a file you changed makes the sync think the file is pristine and overwrite it on the next bundle update. Edit the asset; leave the manifest alone. To restore a bundled default, delete the file and restart.

### Interactive installer

Run the bundled installer for deliberate (re)installation, conflict resolution, and cleanup of orphaned files from older layouts:

```bash
bunx opencode-forge        # or: npx opencode-forge
pnpm run setup             # from a checkout
```

| Flag | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `-f`, `--force` | Overwrite all conflicting files and delete all orphans. |
| `-k`, `--keep` | Keep all local versions; never delete anything. |
| `-y`, `--yes` | Non-interactive: keep edited files, prune orphans. |
| `-n`, `--dry-run` | Report the plan without writing anything. |
| `--no-prune` | Only report orphaned files; never delete them. |

Without a flag the installer is interactive: for each conflicting file it offers overwrite / keep / diff, and for each orphan it offers delete / keep. When you choose **keep** on a conflict, the manifest is updated so future startup syncs continue to preserve your version.

### Plugin-directory install

The installer can also register the plugin in opencode's config directory, instead of hand-editing the `plugins` array:

| Flag | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `--link` | Writes the server shim `<configDir>/plugin/opencode-forge.js`, re-exporting the absolute path of the current build's `dist/index.js`, and the `plugins` entry in `<configDir>/cli.json` pointing at the build's `dist` directory. Because both point at the live build, a rebuild is picked up on the next opencode start with no reinstall. The entry is tied to that checkout path, so it is not portable to another machine. |
| `--vendor` | Copies `package.json`, `forge-config.jsonc`, `dist/`, `container/`, and `skills/` into `<configDir>/plugin/opencode-forge/` (~6.5 MB), writes the server shim re-exporting `./opencode-forge/dist/index.js`, and registers the relative spec `./plugin/opencode-forge/dist` in `cli.json`. The whole config folder becomes self-contained and can be version-controlled and moved to another machine. Requires re-running after an upgrade. |
| `--unlink` | Removes the server shim, the vendored directory, and the `cli.json` entry. |

From a source checkout the same flags are `pnpm run setup --link`, `pnpm run setup --vendor`, and `pnpm run setup --unlink` (the `run` is required — `setup` is a built-in pnpm command). In a non-interactive shell, `--link` and `--vendor` still require one of `-y`, `-f`, or `-k`, matching every other non-interactive use of the installer.

Both modes write the server shim and the `cli.json` entry (see [Plugin loading](#plugin-loading)).

#### Resolved layout

`--link` writes the shim and the `cli.json` entry:

```text
<configDir>/
├── plugin/
│   └── opencode-forge.js           # export { default } from "/abs/path/to/dist/index.js"
└── cli.json                        # plugins: ["/abs/path/to/dist"]
```

`--vendor` copies the whole package:

```text
<configDir>/
├── plugin/
│   ├── opencode-forge.js           # export { default } from "./opencode-forge/dist/index.js"
│   └── opencode-forge/
│       ├── package.json
│       ├── forge-config.jsonc
│       ├── dist/
│       │   ├── index.js
│       │   └── tui.js
│       ├── container/
│       └── skills/
└── cli.json                        # plugins: ["./plugin/opencode-forge/dist"]
```

The vendored copy mirrors the npm package layout rather than being "just dist": forge resolves its bundled assets as siblings of its package root (`container/`, `skills/`, `forge-config.jsonc`), so the sandbox template and the bundled skill sync resolve inside the vendored copy.

#### Plugin loading

Package installs expose `./tui` alongside the server entrypoint, which OpenCode can load automatically from the package entry in `opencode.json`. The config-directory installer uses explicit registrations instead (verified on 2.0.15 and 2.2.2):

- **Server** — the `plugins` array in `opencode.json`/`opencode.jsonc`, or any `*.js` file directly in `<configDir>/plugin/`. The installer uses the second: `opencode-forge.js` is a one-line re-export of the server entry. Package directories under `plugin/`, such as the vendored copy, are not loaded on their own.
- **TUI** — the `plugins` array in `cli.json`, which resolves a directory spec's package entrypoints rather than accepting a file target. That is why the installer points `cli.json` at the built `dist` directory. Path specs resolve relative to the config file's own directory, which makes the vendored `./plugin/opencode-forge/dist` entry portable.

A `cli.json` entry alone loads only the TUI: the sidebar appears but Forge's agents, tools, and hooks do not.

The installer rewrites the shim and updates an existing forge entry in `cli.json` in place, so re-running it is safe. It does not inspect `opencode.json` — if you list forge there and also install it into the config directory, the server loads twice; remove one of them by hand.

#### Verification

`opencode debug config` prints the resolved config. Its `plugins` array should list the forge entry exactly once. `opencode plugin list` should show the shim (`oc-forge`, from `plugin/opencode-forge.js`) and the `cli.json` dist entry.

# Dashboard

Forge's dashboard is a full-screen TUI surface for watching loops, findings, and plans across every project that has Forge data. It is one of the TUI's own routes, not a service: there is no bind address, no HTTP endpoints, no separate process, no browser surface, and no LAN exposure.

Every value comes from the Forge server plugin over the TUI's `FORGE_RPC` contract: `dashboardSummary`, `loopDetail`, `projectFindings`, `amendmentDiff`, `sessionPlan` (with the project id, when reading another project's stored plan), and `planDelete`. The TUI holds no Forge database, so the dashboard also works when the TUI is attached to a remote OpenCode server running Forge.

## Opening the dashboard

Run `Open dashboard` from the command palette (group **Forge**; description "Open the Forge dashboard: loops, findings and plans across all projects"), or use the optional `tui.keybinds.dashboard` binding when one is configured. That binding has no default: when it is empty the command is registered without a shortcut.

Opening records the current TUI route, and when the current session's directory resolves to a project, pre-selects that project. `esc` at the top level — with nothing open or selected — returns to the recorded route.

## Views

Long lists stay bounded: Loops and each Plans block render at most 200 rows, and Findings at most 300, with a "narrow the search to see more" hint when a list is cut off. There is no show-all toggle; search and the status filter are how a list is narrowed. In Findings, the search keeps only the groups of loops it keeps.

### Project list

The first view lists one row per project with Forge data: the union of loop projects and projects with unexecuted plans. A row shows the shortest path label that is unique among projects, the running-loop count, the loop, unexecuted-plan, and bug counts, and the project directory (or the project id when it has no directory).

`/` focuses the search. It matches project paths and labels, loop names and branches, and unexecuted plan titles. A project whose own path or label matches keeps all of its rows; otherwise only its matching loops and plans are kept, and a project with nothing left drops out.

`enter` on a project opens its three sections, each with a count that matches the rows the section lists after the current search: **Loops** counts the matching loops, and **Plans** the matching unexecuted plans plus the matching loops that have a plan. **Findings** shows the project's bug count as `Findings (N bugs)`, because the section body lists bugs and warnings from the on-demand findings read, which may not be loaded yet.

### Loops

Each row shows the loop status, name, current phase (`—` once the loop has completed), an iteration meter, a 1-based section meter (`—` when the loop has no sections), the bug count, cost, duration, and last activity.

- `s` cycles the sort: recent (server order), cost, duration, findings (bug count).
- `f` cycles the status filter: all, running, completed, cancelled, errored, stalled.

### Findings

Findings are grouped per loop in the server's summary order. Each group is headed by the loop name and its finding count, and each finding shows its file and line, description, and scenario when one was recorded. Bugs render `✖`, warnings render `▲`; loops without findings are omitted. `enter` on a group opens that loop.

### Plans

The Plans section lists unexecuted session-scoped plans authored by `plan-write` first, each with its title, age, and character count, followed by executed plans — the loops that have a plan. `enter` on an unexecuted plan shows its stored markdown, fetched on demand. `enter` on an executed plan opens that loop on its Plan tab. Deleting an unexecuted plan is covered under [Deleting plans](#deleting-plans).

### Loop page

`enter` on a loop opens its page. The header shows the status, name, current phase while the loop runs, duration, cost, iteration and section meters (the section meter's label and fill both use the 1-based section number), bug and warning counts, the execution and auditor models (the auditor appends its fallback index when it is non-zero), branch, sandbox on/off, audit and error counts, and any termination reason.

The tabs are Overview, Timeline, Sections (only when the loop has sections), Findings, Plan (only when the loop has a plan), and Usage.

- **Overview:** a phase bar and legend with each phase's duration and percentage, a plan-adjusted callout when the loop's plan was amended, the post-action report (falling back to the completion summary), and the last audit result.
- **Timeline:** a text state-machine diagram of coding → auditing → post_action with per-edge traversal counts and the current phase highlighted while the loop runs, the phase bar and legend, the most recent transitions, and a merged timeline of transitions and plan amendments.
- **Sections:** the section list with each section's status, an `adjusted` marker when the plan changed it, duration, and attempt count; `enter` expands its captured done/deviations/follow-ups and stored section plan.
- **Findings:** the current findings grouped by section, with severity.
- **Plan:** the stored plan markdown and its amendments; `j`/`k` selects an amendment, `enter` loads and expands its before/after diff.
- **Usage:** totals (cost, tokens, message count), then role-split bars, token-composition bars, and cost-by-model bars.

## Key bindings

Dashboard page:

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `↑` / `↓`, `j` / `k` | Move the selection |
| `enter` | Open the selected row |
| `/` | Focus the search |
| `esc` | Blur the search, else close an open plan, else deselect the project, else return to the previous route |
| `tab` / `shift+tab` | Cycle sections |
| `1`-`3` | Jump to Loops, Findings, Plans |
| `s` | Cycle the sort (Loops only) |
| `f` | Cycle the status filter (Loops only) |
| `d` | Delete the selected unexecuted plan (Plans only) |
| `r` | Refresh everything the current page shows |

While the search is focused, the move, open, section, sort, filter, delete, and refresh keys are disabled; `esc` blurs the search.

Loop page:

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `tab` / `shift+tab` | Cycle tabs |
| `↑` / `↓` | Scroll one line |
| `pgup` / `pgdn` | Scroll one viewport |
| `j` / `k` | Move the selection in Sections and Plan |
| `enter` | Toggle a section's details or an amendment diff |
| `r` | Refresh everything the current page shows |
| `esc` | Return to the dashboard |

## Live updates

The dashboard never polls. It refetches when the server pushes `loopsChanged` or `plansChanged` for a project, and re-reads everything after the event stream reconnects. While no dashboard page is mounted, those pushes only mark cached state stale, so a closed dashboard never fetches.

Those events come only from Forge plugin instances loaded in the same OpenCode server process. A change written by another OpenCode process that shares the same Forge database is not pushed. Reopening the dashboard refreshes the project summary only; cached findings and an open loop page keep their old data until you press `r`, which refreshes everything the current page shows.

## Deleting plans

Only unexecuted session-scoped plans can be deleted, from the Plans section with `d`. The TUI opens the plan, asks for confirmation naming it and stating that the deletion cannot be undone, then sends `planDelete`. A cancelled or failed delete leaves the plan open (a failure also shows an error toast); a successful delete closes it and refreshes the summary. Executed plans have no delete action.

## Removed: the former standalone dashboard

Forge previously shipped the dashboard as a separate standalone server. That server, its separate start script, its HTTP endpoints, and the `dashboard` config block (`dashboard.host` / `dashboard.port`) are gone; the dashboard exists only as the TUI surface described above. A leftover `dashboard` key in `forge-config.jsonc` is ignored rather than rejected, because the config loader does not validate unknown top-level keys.

See also: [Configuration → TUI](configuration.md#tui), [TUI](tui.md), [Loop System](loop-system.md).

# Loop System Documentation

The loop system provides autonomous iterative development with automatic code auditing.

## Loop Lifecycle Rules

### Plugin Boot Behavior

- **Plugin boot does not mutate loop rows.** Initialization loads storage and runtime services only.
- No loops are recovered, cancelled, restarted, or reconciled during plugin startup.
- Loop recovery and restart are explicit user actions via `loop-status restart=true`.

### Restartability

- **Any non-completed loop is restartable** via explicit restart when the worktree is available.
- Restartable statuses: `running`, `cancelled`, `errored`, `stalled`.
- **Completed loops are history-only** and cannot be restarted.
- **A missing worktree blocks restart only when the scratch branch is gone too** — if the branch survives, restart recreates the worktree from it (`git worktree add <branch>`); when both are gone the work is unrecoverable.

### Restart Semantics

- Restart preserves loop identity, plan, worktree path, section progress, review findings, and per-loop sandbox settings (a loop launched with the sandbox off stays off; its resource overrides apply if the sandbox is recreated).
- Restart resets the iteration count to 1 and clears the error budget.
- Restart creates a fresh session and preserves the section index. An ordinary `auditing` phase restarts as `coding`, while an enabled `post_action` phase is preserved. Any standby session is discarded, so a restart never resumes retained context.
- Restart marks any pending handoff `discarded`, so the loop starts fresh with no turn record carried over from before the restart.
- Restarts into section coding with outstanding bug findings for the current section use the continuation prompt, including full finding details and the shared remediation policy; without current-section bugs, they use the initial section prompt.

### Stale Workspace Sweep

- Stale workspace sweep is **teardown cleanup-only**, not boot-time recovery.
- Sweep removes workspace registrations for non-running restartable loops (`cancelled`, `errored`, `stalled`) while preserving worktrees for manual restart.
- Completed loops are fully removed (registration + worktree).
- Running loops are never touched by sweep.

## Loop Lifecycle

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Coding: loop tool invoked
    Coding --> Auditing: loop-handoff
    Auditing --> Coding: loop-handoff, findings remain, retry section
    Auditing --> Coding: loop-handoff, clean, next section
    Auditing --> PostAction: loop-handoff, clean, no section left, post-action configured
    note right of PostAction: Only when loop.postAction.enabled and a non-empty skill or prompt is set
    Auditing --> [*]: loop-handoff, clean, no section left
    PostAction --> [*]: loop-complete
    Coding --> [*]: 3 turns without loop-handoff (handoff_missing, errored) / max iterations / stall timeout / cancellation
    Auditing --> [*]: 3 turns without loop-handoff (handoff_missing, errored)
    PostAction --> [*]: 3 turns without loop-complete (completed)
```

### Phases

A loop has three persisted phases:

1. **`coding`** — a code session works on the current section or plan.
2. **`auditing`** — the auditor reviews the current section (or the whole change for a non-sectioned plan loop) against conventions and stored findings. A clean section audit advances to the next section, or completes the loop — into `post_action` when configured — when no section is still open.
3. **`post_action`** — an optional best-effort action after a clean audit.

Each completed code or audit pass rotates to a fresh session, except that a reusable standby session is resumed on same-section phase switches in both directions — coding → auditing and dirty audit → coding (see [Session Rotation](#session-rotation)); a new section always starts fresh. Audit findings feed back into the next coding iteration.

## Loop States

Each loop has a `LoopState` backed by the typed `loops` and `loop_large_fields` SQLite tables:

```typescript
interface LoopState {
  active: boolean                    // Whether loop is currently running
  sessionId: string                  // Current OpenCode session ID
  standbySessionId?: string          // Retained session for the next same-scope retry
  loopName: string                   // Unique loop identifier
  worktreeDir: string                // Worktree path
  projectDir?: string                // Project directory path
  worktreeBranch?: string            // Branch name if using worktree
  iteration: number                  // Current iteration count
  maxIterations: number              // Maximum iterations (0 = unlimited)
  startedAt: string                  // ISO timestamp
  prompt?: string                    // Original task prompt
  phase: 'coding' | 'auditing' | 'post_action'
  lastAuditResult?: string           // Last audit output
  errorCount: number                 // Consecutive error count
  auditCount: number                 // Number of audits completed
  terminationReason?: string         // Reason for termination
  completedAt?: string               // ISO timestamp
  worktree?: boolean                 // Whether using worktree isolation
  modelFailed?: boolean              // Whether model error occurred
  sandbox?: boolean                  // Whether using msb sandbox
  sandboxContainer?: string          // Sandbox name if sandboxed
  completionSummary?: string         // Summary of loop completion
  executionModel?: string            // Model used for execution
  auditorModel?: string              // Model used for auditing
  auditorFallbackIndex?: number      // Index into the auditor model fallback chain
  workspaceId?: string               // OpenCode workspace ID
  hostSessionId?: string             // Host session ID for post-completion redirect
  currentSectionIndex: number
  totalSections: number
}
```

Per-turn output lives in `loop_handoffs`, not on the loop row: only the current record is `pending`, it resolves to `applied` or `discarded`, and the resolved rows remain as history. `lastAuditResult` and `completionSummary` on the loop row are display text, never decision input.

## Handoff-Driven Turn Ends

A phase turn ends only through a persisted handoff row written by `loop-handoff` (coding, auditing) or `loop-complete` (post-action). The runtime never parses assistant text for decisions, summaries, markers, or completion. The audit verdict comes only from the findings store, and post-action completion only from the recorded `loop-complete` payload.

### `loop_handoffs`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `id` | integer | Auto-incrementing primary key |
| `project_id`, `loop_name` | text | Loop identity; the foreign key `(project_id, loop_name)` references `loops` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, so deleting a loop removes its handoffs |
| `session_id` | text | Session that recorded the handoff |
| `role` | text | `coder`, `auditor`, or `post_action` (`CHECK` constraint) |
| `phase` | text | Phase at write time: `coding`, `auditing`, or `post_action` |
| `section_index` | integer / null | Current section for sectioned loops, `null` for non-sectioned plan loops |
| `iteration` | integer | Loop iteration at write time |
| `payload` | JSON text | Strictly validated role payload |
| `status` | text | `pending`, `applied`, or `discarded` (`CHECK` constraint) |
| `created_at`, `resolved_at` | integer | Write and resolution timestamps; `resolved_at` is `null` while pending |

A partial unique index (`idx_loop_handoffs_pending`) allows at most one `pending` row per loop, and a history index (`idx_loop_handoffs_loop`) keeps every resolved row in id order. Resolution is a single guarded update: marking a row `applied` matches on the recording `session_id`, the expected `role`, and `status = 'pending'`, and discarding matches `status = 'pending'`, so a record resolves exactly once.

Every payload is validated strictly against its role schema once on write, by `parseHandoffWriteInput` inside `recordHandoff` (the repository stores the already-validated payload and does not validate again before the insert), and on every read (`mapHandoffRow`). An invalid row is logged and skipped; its payload is never coerced or partially applied.

- **Coder payload** — `changes` (`{ summary, reason }`, at least one), `deviations` (`{ planItem, actual, reason }`), `verification` (`{ command, cwd, outcome: 'pass' | 'fail' | 'not-run', changedAfter }`, at least one), and optional `notes`.
- **Auditor payload** — optional `summary` (`{ done, deviations, followUps }`) and optional `notes`. `summary` is required for a clean section audit, forbidden while blocking bug findings remain, and forbidden in non-sectioned loops.
- **Post-action payload** — `outcome` (`completed`, `completed_with_issues`, or `failed`), `steps` (`{ name, status: 'done' | 'skipped' | 'failed', detail? }`, at least one), `followUps`, and optional `notes`.

Recording rules:

- Only the loop's current session may record a handoff; any other session is rejected.
- The tool must match the phase: `loop-handoff` in coding and auditing, `loop-complete` in post-action. The wrong tool is rejected.
- The call is rejected while any other loop session, subagents included, is busy or retrying, and rejected when that session status cannot be verified.
- The last call in the same turn replaces the earlier pending record instead of adding a second one.
- A successful call does not advance the loop. It only stores the record; the phase runner applies it when the turn ends.

Turn-end sequence:

1. In coding and auditing, a persisted provider-limit error is classified first and either terminates the loop or advances the auditor fallback chain.
2. The persisted assistant error is charged to the phase's error budget next: a model error marks the model as failed, and the third consecutive error terminates with `error_max_retries`. The turn then defers while any loop session other than the standby — the current session included — is busy or retrying, or a prompt is still queued in the session inbox. The deferral fails closed: a session status that cannot be verified keeps the turn deferred. In coding and auditing this wait runs before the phase acts on an assistant error, so an errored turn rotates only after every other loop session has settled. Post-action is the exception: an assistant error applies any pending record and completes best-effort before the wait.
3. `applyPendingHandoff` runs scoped to the current session and role and applies the record atomically, once, only while it is `pending`.

With a record the runner proceeds to `nextTransition`; a repeat resolution or a row recorded by a different session yields nothing. A pending row recorded by this session for the other role is left pending and logged, so the role that wrote it stays the one to apply it. Without a record:

- A turn with no reply at all — its last message role is `none` or `user` — is re-sent the full phase prompt.
- Any other turn receives the short nudge "You ended your turn without calling `loop-handoff`/`loop-complete`. Finish the work, then call it.", including one whose assistant reply was cut off (`finish` reason `length` or `tool-calls`).
- Each phase turn gets 3 nudges (`MAX_HANDOFF_NUDGES`); the count resets whenever a session is activated or the phase changes, including when a reused standby session is activated, so a previous turn's spent nudges never shorten the new turn's budget.
- After the third nudge the next idle ends the turn: coding and auditing terminate with `terminationReason: 'handoff_missing'` and status `errored`, while post-action completes as `completed`.

An abort-and-resend the loop itself initiates — auditor model fallback after a provider limit, or the busy-stall continue nudge — discards the pending handoff recorded in the aborted turn, so the resent turn starts with no record.

**Coding.** A `coder` record is stored as the attempt's decisions through `handoffCompletionKey(record)` and its rendered `formatCoderHandoff` output, then the `coder-handoff` transition rotates to auditing. An assistant error still rotates to audit, with no decisions recorded and no nudge.

**Auditing.** A non-abort audit session error discards the pending auditor handoff before rotating back to coding, without incrementing the audit count; an aborted audit turn that already holds an `auditor` record for the session is processed as a handoff instead. A clean section audit whose pending record carries no `summary` is discarded and the auditor is nudged rather than completing the section. With an `auditor` record the verdict comes only from the findings store, never from the payload; `lastAuditResult` is rendered from the payload and the verdict for display, and transition rows are logged as `auditor-handoff`: advancing to the next section, returning to the same dirty section, continuing a dirty non-sectioned audit, or entering post-action.

**Post-action.** A `post_action` record sets `postActionReport` from `formatPostActionReport` and `completionSummary` from `formatPostActionSummary`, then completes the loop. An assistant error applies any pending record best-effort and completes. The loop status is always `completed` regardless of the reported outcome, but a failed send of a post-action nudge goes through the normal prompt-error handling, so it can end the loop with `provider_limit` or count toward `error_max_retries`.

## Session Rotation

Each phase switch runs in a **fresh session** to keep context small and prioritize speed, unless the loop resumes its standby (see below):

1. **Coding phase** completes
2. New session is created
3. Continuation prompt is injected with:
   - Original task prompt
   - Current iteration number
   - Audit findings (if any)
4. The previous session is deleted once its usage is captured, unless the loop retained it as the standby

**Standby session.** `loops.standby_session_id` (migration 155) records at most one retained session, always the role opposite the current phase. It is the only way a loop resumes a session it had switched away from.

- When coding finishes and a fresh audit session is created, the coder becomes the standby — unless a bug finding has reached the recurrence escalation threshold, in which case it is deleted instead.
- When a dirty audit sends work back to coding, the coder is resumed from the standby instead of a new session, and the audit session becomes the standby in turn (an audit session that errored is deleted instead). A sectioned loop only ever reuses within the same section: a clean section audit releases the standby before the next section's fresh coder session. A non-sectioned loop reuses the standby across its audit iterations.
- Reuse requires `inspectReusableStandby` to pass: the standby is not the current session, still exists with messages, has no bug finding at the recurrence escalation threshold (`RECURRENCE_ESCALATION_THRESHOLD`, 3), and its role's reuse percentage is not `0` (`loop.sessionReuse.coderContextPercent` / `auditorContextPercent`, default 50 each; `0` disables reuse for that role). The role comes from the standby: the coder session while auditing, the audit session while coding. When its last assistant turn's context (input plus cache read/write) reached that percentage of the model's context window, the standby is not rejected: `inspectStandbyCandidate` marks it `needsCompaction`, and the loop queues a `session.compact` before the follow-up prompt so the host compacts the session first and the prompt runs in the same session against the summary. A compaction that cannot be enqueued falls back to the fresh-session path for that role. An unknown context window — no model on the message, a failed lookup, or no positive `limit.context` — allows reuse without compaction. Recurrence escalation forces a fresh session for both roles. When reuse fails, the loop rotates to a fresh session and captures the standby's usage before deleting it; the audit session is still retained as the next standby even when it is over its threshold, because it will be compacted when reused.
- A resumed coder receives `buildCoderFollowUpPrompt` — the loop notice, the open findings, and the coder handoff instruction — not the full plan; its earlier context still applies, co

The phase completes when the post-action session records `loop-complete`, with a best-effort completion when 3 turns pass without one or when the session ends on an assistant error; see [Behavior](#behavior) for the record handling behind both paths.

## Termination

In addition to a clean audit, the loop terminates when:

- **Max iterations** — The `maxIterations` cap is exceeded (0 = unlimited).
- **Stall timeout** — After `maxConsecutiveStalls` consecutive stalls (default: 5). Use `loop-status` with `restart` to resume from the persisted section and iteration.
- **Consecutive errors** — 3 consecutive errors in either phase.
- **Missing handoff** — 3 turns in coding or auditing without a `loop-handoff` record terminate with `terminationReason: 'handoff_missing'`; a post-action turn without `loop-complete` completes instead.

## Post-Completion Action Phase

After a clean audit (the clean section audit that completes a sectioned loop, `audit-clear` for non-sectioned plan loops), before worktree teardown, the loop may run a **post-completion action** configured via `loop.postAction` in `forge-config.jsonc`. This phase is best-effort — it is not re-audited. When a skill is configured, that skill's unattended workflow governs its fixes and validation; without one, it relies only on safe, scoped fixes. The post-action runs as the `code` agent in a fresh session inside the worktree.

```jsonc
{
  "loop": {
    "postAction": {
      "enabled": false,       // Enable the post-completion action phase
      "skill": "pr-review",   // Skill to load via the Skill tool (e.g. "pr-review")
      "prompt": "..."         // Extra instruction text; used standalone when no skill is set
    }
  }
}
```

### Configuration

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `loop.postAction.enabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Enable the post-completion action phase. |
| `loop.postAction.skill` | `string` | — | Name of a skill to load via the Skill tool at action time (e.g. `"pr-review"`). Must be installed host-side. |
| `loop.postAction.prompt` | `string` | — | Optional extra instruction text appended to the action prompt. Used standalone when no skill is set. |
| `loop.postAction.model` | `string` | — | Optional `provider/model` for the post-action session, sent without a variant. Falls back to the loop's auditor model — with the auditor's variant — when unset or when the configured model fails. |

### Behavior

- Runs only after a clean audit completes (the clean section audit that completes a sectioned loop, `audit-clear` for non-sectioned plan loops).
- Runs **inside the worktree** as the `code` agent, with access to the full worktree state (including uncommitted changes).
- **Best-effort:** The post-action result is not re-audited. When a skill is configured, that skill's unattended workflow governs the fixes and validation; without one, the phase applies only safe, scoped fixes. The question tool is blocked — any finding requiring clarification is auto-deferred.
- **Completion record:** The prompt requires the agent to finish every step (subagents, merges, saved records) and then call `loop-complete` with `outcome`, one `steps` entry per workflow step, `followUps`, and optional `notes`. When the session goes idle, Forge first waits until every loop session, subagents included, is not busy or retrying and no prompt is queued in the session inbox, then applies the pending record; a session that stays busy is left to the watchdog's stall handling. An assistant error skips that wait: it applies any pending record and completes best-effort. Without a record it nudges up to 3 times, then completes best-effort; a post-action nudge that cannot be sent goes through the normal prompt-error handling rather than completing.
- An applied record completes the loop normally, including one recorded in response to a nudge.
- An aborted post-action session with a pending record processes that record; without one, the loop completes with no report.
- If the post-action session fails to create, the loop completes as `completed` without retrying, and no record is applied.
- **Outcome capture:** `postActionReport` is the rendered `formatPostActionReport` of the applied `loop-complete` payload, and `completion_summary` is `formatPostActionSummary` of the same payload. `loop-status` and the [TUI dashboard](dashboard.md) prefer the **Post-Action Report** and fall back to the **Completion Summary** when no report was captured. Both are captured only when a record is applied, including an assistant-error completion that has one; a completion without a record leaves them empty. The loop status is **always** `completed` regardless of what the post-action reported — the plan itself was already cleared by the audit; the report only provides context (alternate-review verdict, CI result, etc.).

## Cancellation

Loops can be cancelled via:
- `loop-cancel` tool
- `/loop-cancel` slash command

Cancellation:
1. Marks loop as inactive
2. Sets `terminationReason` to `'cancelled'`
3. Stops sandbox if applicable
4. Optionally cleans up worktree (if `cleanupWorktree: true`)
5. Discards any pending handoff (termination marks it `discarded`)

## Error Handling

| Error Type | Behavior |
|------------|----------|
| Model error | Automatic fallback to default model, retry |
| Error retry limit | Loop terminates with `terminationReason: 'error_max_retries'` |
| Missing handoff | Loop terminates with `terminationReason: 'handoff_missing'` after 3 turns without a handoff |
| Stall timeout | Loop terminates with `terminationReason: 'stall_timeout'` after the configured consecutive stall limit |

## Model Configuration

Model and variant selection follows this priority order (first match wins):

**Execution model:**

1. In-session dialog override (instance lifetime)
2. `config.executionModel`
3. Last-used loop preference
4. Platform default

**Auditor model:**

1. In-session dialog override (instance lifetime)
2. `config.auditorModel`
3. `config.executionModel`
4. Last-used auditor model
5. Last-used execution model
6. Platform default

Variants use override → matching config value → last-used loop value. The auditor variant does not inherit the execution variant. When launching from the TUI dialog, your selection is remembered and pre-filled on subsequent launches, and the dialog allows selecting a separate model for the auditor phase. On model errors during execution, automatic fallback to the default model kicks in.

## Management

- **Slash commands**: `/execute-plan` to start, `/loop-cancel` to cancel.
- **Tools**: `execute-plan` to start with parameters, `loop-status` for checking progress (with restart capability), `loop-cancel` to cancel.
- **Loop names**: a new loop start reserves a unique name (`src/loop/name-uniqueness.ts`) and that has no live `forge/<name>` branch, taking a `-N` suffix; a restart reuses its own name and branch. A caller-chosen branch, passed through `FORGE_RPC.executePlan` as `branch`, is used instead of `forge/<name>`, while the name reservation still checks the generated `forge/<name>` slug.
- **Cleanup**: terminal loops and their loop-scoped plans are swept automatically once `completedLoopTtlMs` passes after completion. Session-scoped plans have no TTL and are removed by `bun scripts/cleanup-plans.ts [--older-than=30d] [--project=<id>] [--dry-run]` (bulk purge) or from the [TUI dashboard](dashboard.md)'s Plans section (select the plan and press `d`); `bun scripts/cleanup-loop.ts <loopName>` removes one loop's row, its plans, worktree, and sandbox, and deletes the persisted branch when it starts with `forge/`; a caller-chosen branch outside that prefix is kept and reported. These scripts are source-checkout only.

## Tool Restrictions

Inside active loop sessions:
- `git push` is not denied by default; add a scoped `loop.permissions.deny` entry such as `{ "permission": "bash", "pattern": "git push *" }` to deny it
- `execute-plan` is blocked (tool hooks)
- `question` is blocked (tool hooks)

# Sandbox

Forge can run loop iterations or one selected host session inside an isolated `msb` sandbox — a microVM booted by the [microsandbox](https://microsandbox.dev) CLI — while keeping the active project directory mounted at its identical host path for fast host/sandbox file sharing.

See also: [Configuration](configuration.md), [Tools](tools.md), [Loop System](loop-system.md).

## Prerequisites

- The `msb` CLI installed — there is **no account and no login step**. Install with:
  ```bash
  curl -fsSL https://install.microsandbox.dev | sh
  ```
  Verify the host is ready with `msb doctor` (an alias of `msb self doctor`), which checks the hypervisor prerequisites. The interactive installer (`bunx opencode-forge`, or `pnpm run setup` from a checkout) offers to run this command for you when it cannot find `msb` on `PATH`.
- A host that can run microVMs: Linux with KVM or macOS on Apple silicon. msb advertises Windows 11 with Windows Hypervisor Platform, but Forge's sandbox shell routing relies on a POSIX s
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
gain, so the agent is not left reading container output as if it described the host.

`memory` and `cpus` are exactly what the guest gets. There is no autoscaling: nothing observes memory pressure, so a build needing more than `memory` is OOM-killed rather than given more. Size `memory` for the peak of the heaviest command the sandbox will run.

msb's `--max-memory`/`--max-cpus` ceilings are deliberately not exposed. They only reserve hotplug capacity that must be claimed explicitly with `msb modify --memory <size>` from the **host**; agents run inside the sandbox and cannot call `msb`, so a ceiling never rescues a failing in-sandbox build.

Forge reuses existing running or stopped sandboxes rather than recreating them. Changing these config values does not resize an existing loop sandbox; remove it (`msb rm <sandbox>`) so the next run creates it with the new values, or resize it in place with `msb modify`. The host sandbox converges to its overrides over config the next time it is validated after a restart.

# Common Issues

See also: [Workspace Integration](workspaces.md), [Sandbox](sandbox.md), [Configuration](configuration.md).

## Worktree execution fails to start

**Most common cause:** the project has no root commit. Worktree loops require a git repository with at least one commit; OpenCode scopes its instance to project `global` when started in a directory without one. The `guardCommittedProject` precondition rejects the launch with `bad_request` (400) and a "Loop start blocked" error toast before any worktree or session is created:

> No git commit in this project — the loop session would be invisible to this opencode instance. Commit, restart opencode, and retry.

Symptoms include:

- A plan loop or TUI Loop launch fails immediately with a `bad_request` (400), before its first coding session starts
- A "Loop start blocked" error toast
- No loop worktree appears in the sidebar

Create an initial commit, restart OpenCode, and retry.

**Separate failure — internal workspace creation:** once the git precondition passes, worktree creation can still fail inside the workspace layer. That is a different fault, surfaces as `internal_error` (500), and is logged as `handleStartLoop: failed to create builtin worktree workspace`, sometimes preceded by `createBuiltinWorktreeWorkspace: workspace.create returned no workspace id`. Investigate the worktree/workspace layer rather than the git state.

## Workspace prerequisites

Worktree loops require a git repository with at least one commit. If OpenCode started before the initial commit, it resolves the project as `global`; create the commit, restart OpenCode, and retry.

# Planning and Execution Workflow

Plan with a smart model, execute with a fast model. The architect agent researches the codebase and designs an implementation plan; the code agent implements it.

See also: [Agents and Slash Commands](agents-and-commands.md), [Tools](tools.md), [Loop System](loop-system.md), [TUI](tui.md).

## How Plans Work

The interactive architect captures the request (restating it in chat), researches the codebase, then settles the route before designing: it calls the `question` tool with one grouped set of questions that settles the route — one per decision group (placement and ownership, reuse versus extending versus new code, data and interface shape, edge-case and error policy, sequencing, verification strategy, plus any group research surfaced), each with 2–4 research-backed options and the recommended one first — and repeats a fresh grouped round after each answer set, re-researching newly opened paths, until every route decision is settled. It restates the outcome and the chosen 
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
config. In-session changes in the dialog override all other sources and persist for the OpenCode instance lifetime only (not across restarts).

For New session and Execute here, execution is immediate — there are no additional LLM calls between approval and execution. The system intercepts the user's approval answer, reads the cached plan, and dispatches it programmatically to the code agent. The architect never processes the approval response. For Loop mode the path depends on the surface: the TUI execution dialog dispatches the loop directly, while the question-based plan approval instructs the architect to launch it with the `execute-plan` tool.

## Troubleshooting

- **No plan found** — Ensure the architect called `plan-write` in the current session and completed the stored plan.
- **TUI shows no plan** — Plans are session-scoped on the server; switch to the session where the architect produced the plan.
- **Need logs** — Set `logging.enabled` to `true`, and optionally `logging.debug` for verbose output.

# Workspace Integration

Forge worktree loops run in native OpenCode worktrees and locations: each loop gets its own worktree directory, registered in the project's worktree inventory, and the sidebar lists the project's active loops.

See also: [Loop System](loop-system.md), [Architecture](architecture.md), [Common Issues](troubleshooting.md).

## Requirements

Worktrees and locations are first-class in OpenCode 2.x, so there is no experimental runtime toggle, no environment variable, and no version floor. The only prerequisite is the repository requirement below.

All worktree-based execution paths require a git repository with at least one root commit: `execute-plan` (Loop mode) and TUI Loop execution dialog launches check for the root commit before creating worktrees or sessions. If OpenCode started before the initial commit, it resolves the project as `global`; create the commit, restart OpenCode, and retry.

## How it works

When a worktree loop starts, Forge:

1. Creates the git worktree through its ow
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
ewhere, and `git rev-parse` for the base ref. A worktree registration whose directory was deleted without `git worktree prune` is marked prunable by git and does not count as holding the branch. Forge never fetches, so a `baseRef` must already resolve locally. Restart and workspace recovery re-create the worktree from the persisted `worktreeBranch` with no base ref, so a loop continues on the same branch at its tip; when another checkout holds that branch they fail with `Branch <branch> is checked out in worktree <path>; choose another branch or free it`.

## Failure behavior

If initial worktree creation fails at startup — API mismatch or a network error — the loop aborts before creating the first loop session. If a worktree disappears after a loop is already running, Forge attempts to re-provision or detach it and continue where possible.

## From the TUI

Loops are launched from the execution dialog (or the `execute-plan` tool); each loop runs in its worktree directory, and the sidebar lists active loops.
